title: The comma that breaks tuning — drawn, generated, and measured

sub: And the gap is why every piano you have ever heard
is deliberately, slightly out of tune.

cards.title: FIVE WORDS, IN PLAIN ENGLISH
items: the same note higher — double the frequency
the next simplest step: three halves the frequency
one hundredth of a semitone; twelve hundred to an octave
two close pitches pulsing against each other

cards.title: WHY THOSE TWO RATIOS AND NOT OTHERS
items: one pitch plus quiet copies at 2x, 3x, 4x…
every one of its parts already exists below
the next-best match, and the strongest after the octave
the parts land on each other instead of near each other

a pure fifth is very slightly WIDER than seven semitones

cards.title: SO WHY IS A PIANO OUT OF TUNE
items: no piano is tuned in pure intervals
is left about fourteen cents wide
every key sounds the same, and you can change key
a faint roughness in every third, everywhere

lines: The circle of fifths is not a circle.
is what to do about that.
cards.kicker: Built, rendered and measured in DAW Pro.

stages.narration: Here is a fact that sounds like a mistake. If you take the interval musicians call a perfect fifth, the purest-sounding step there is after the octave, and you stack twelve of them one on top of another, you should land exactly seven octaves above where you started. The arithmetic of Western music says you do. You do not. You land a little bit sharp — by a gap that has a name, the Pythagorean comma, and consequences that reach every instrument with fixed pitches on it. This lesson does three things with that gap. It draws it, so you can see twelve fifths walk round a circle and fail to come home. It generates it as sound and measures it, so the number is confirmed by its own material rather than quoted at you. And then it shows you what musicians decided to do about it, which is the reason every piano you have ever heard is deliberately, very slightly, out of tune. All of it is built, rendered and measured in DAW Pro. Nothing here is generated by a music model, and nothing here is a number I read somewhere.

Five words first, in plain English, because the rest of this depends on them and none of them are hard. An interval is just the distance between two pitches. An octave is the interval you get when you double a frequency — the same note, higher, and it sounds so much like the same note that we give it the same letter. A fifth is the next simplest step after that: multiply the frequency by three halves. On a piano it is seven white-and-black keys up, A to E. A cent is a unit for measuring how far apart two pitches are. There are one hundred cents in a semitone and twelve hundred cents in an octave, and a trained ear starts to notice a difference at somewhere around five of them. And beating is what you hear when two pitches are very close but not the same: the sound pulses, getting louder and quieter, over and over. That pulsing is going to be this lesson's measuring instrument, so we will come back to it properly.

Why those two ratios in particular, and not any of the others. When almost anything real makes a note — a string, a reed, a voice — it does not produce one frequency. It produces a whole stack of them: the pitch you name, and then quieter copies at exactly two times, three times, four times that frequency, and on up. Those copies are called harmonics, and they are why a violin and a trumpet playing the same note sound completely different. Now put two notes together. If the second note's frequency is exactly double the first, every single harmonic it has already exists in the first note's stack. Nothing new, nothing clashing. That is the octave, and it is why it sounds like the same note. Three to two is the next best thing: not a perfect containment, but the two stacks line up over and over, one landing on the other. That is a fifth, and what you are about to hear is a pure one — four hundred and forty hertz against six hundred and sixty, rendered by the app. Listen to how still it is. Nothing moves.

To compare intervals we need a ruler, and the ruler is the cent. Twelve hundred cents to an octave, one hundred to a semitone. It is a logarithmic ruler, which just means that the same number of cents is the same musical distance whether you are up at the top of the keyboard or down at the bottom, even though the number of hertz involved is wildly different. Measured that way, a pure fifth — that three to two ratio — is seven hundred and one point nine five five cents. Look at that number for a second. Seven semitones would be exactly seven hundred. So a pure fifth is not seven semitones. It is seven semitones plus a bit under two cents. That bit under two cents is almost nothing on its own. It is far too small to hear as a mistuned note. But it is the entire subject of this lesson, because we are about to do it twelve times in a row.

So let us do it, and watch. In a moment you will see a circle. The whole way round it is one octave — twelve hundred cents, with a mark every hundred, one per semitone. We start on A, at the top. Then we take one pure fifth, which moves us seven marks round and very slightly past. Then another, and another, twelve of them, and each time the line spirals out one ring so you can see where it has been. The letters are the notes each fifth lands on: A, E, B, F sharp, and round through all twelve of them. Underneath, you will hear every one of those thirteen pitches, in order, rendered by the app. Listen for the last note especially. It is supposed to be the A we started on, seven octaves later, folded back down. And when the line gets there, it does not come home. It lands just past the mark it started on. And when that gap appears on screen, you will hear the two pitches it sits between played together — the A we set off from, and the A twelve pure fifths landed on. Hold on to what that sounds like, because measuring it is what the rest of this lesson does.

Here is the same thing as arithmetic, and it is short. Stacking fifths means multiplying by three halves, so twelve fifths is three halves multiplied by itself twelve times. Seven octaves is two multiplied by itself seven times. If the two were equal, the circle would close. They are not. Divide one by the other and you get five hundred and thirty one thousand, four hundred and forty one, over five hundred and twenty four thousand, two hundred and eighty eight. Not one. Close to one — about one point zero one four — but not one. Converted into cents, that overshoot is twenty three point four six cents. Slightly less than a quarter of a semitone. That is the Pythagorean comma. It is not a measurement error and it is not something that could be fixed with better instruments. It is a fact about the numbers two and three: no whole number of one will ever equal a whole number of the other. On screen is the same walk drawn as a ladder — where the arithmetic says each of the thirteen pitches should sit, and, crossed on top of it, where the app actually rendered them.

It is worth saying exactly how the sounds in this film were made, because the whole argument rests on them being right. There are exactly two audio files, and both were generated once, at four hundred and forty point zero zero zero hertz. One is a pure sine wave, and it makes the walk and the two A's. The other is a sawtooth — a buzzier wave, with strong harmonics — and it makes the fifths and the thirds, because the beating in those lives between harmonics, and a sine wave does not have any. Each one is loaded into the app's sampler as a zone, and a zone has a tune control, measured in cents. On screen now is the zone that makes a pure fifth: the file is the sawtooth, and the tune knob reads plus seven hundred and two cents. Every single pitch you hear in this lesson is one of those two files with a different number in that box. Nothing is a preset, nothing is a recording of an instrument. Then every render was measured back, by finding the peak of its frequency spectrum. Across all twenty one measurements — the thirteen in the walk you just heard, and the eight in the comparisons still to come — the largest disagreement between what the arithmetic asked for and what came out of the app is zero, to four decimal places, in cents. So when this lesson tells you two tones are a given distance apart, that is not a setting. It is a measurement.

Now the measuring instrument, because from here on this lesson stops asserting things and starts counting them. When two tones are close in pitch but not identical, their waves drift through each other. Sometimes a peak of one lines up with a peak of the other and they add up to something twice as loud. A moment later that same peak has slid onto a trough, and they cancel. That cycle — loud, quiet, loud, quiet — is called beating, and here is the useful part: the number of pulses per second is exactly the difference between the two frequencies in hertz. Two tones six hertz apart pulse six times a second. You can count them with a stopwatch. In a moment you will see the two waves drawn, and the sum of them underneath, with a bar showing how loud that sum is at each instant. The first half is two A's at exactly the same pitch, and nothing moves at all. Then one of them goes sharp by the comma, and everything moves.

So let us hold the comma up against it. Four hundred and forty hertz on its own, and four hundred and forty six point zero zero three — which is four hundred and forty raised by exactly twenty three point four six cents. The comma, turned into a pitch. Subtract one from the other and the prediction is six point zero zero three pulses a second. Measured off the render, by taking the amplitude envelope and finding its strongest rate: six point zero zero three. And it is deep — the pulsing swings the level by point nine four out of a possible one, which means it very nearly drops to silence at the bottom of every pulse. The control matters more than the measurement, though. The before half of this comparison is two tones at exactly the same pitch, same instrument, same level, in exactly the same arrangement. Its measured depth is zero to four decimal places. So when you hear the after half pulsing, the pulsing is the twenty three cents and nothing else. You are listening to the Pythagorean comma directly.

So what do you do about a circle that does not close. For a very long time the answer was: pick your favourite keys, keep those intervals pure, and shove the entire error into one interval you promise never to play. That interval was called the wolf, because of the noise it made, and it meant some keys were beautiful and others were unusable. The answer that eventually won is much simpler and much stranger. Take the whole comma, divide it into twelve equal pieces, and make every single fifth that much narrower. One twelfth of twenty three point four six is one point nine five five cents. Take that off every fifth and a fifth becomes exactly seven hundred cents — exactly seven semitones — and twelve of them come to exactly seven octaves. That is equal temperament, and it is what the piano in every room you have ever been in is tuned to. Watch the same walk again with that one change, and listen: the thirteenth note is now four hundred and forty hertz, measured, and it is the note we started on.

Nothing is free, so here is the bill, and this is where the beating earns its keep. A tempered fifth is not a pure fifth any more. Four hundred and forty hertz against six hundred and fifty nine point two five five, instead of six hundred and sixty. Those two are over two hundred hertz apart, far too far apart to beat directly — but their harmonics are not. The lower note's third harmonic sits at thirteen hundred and twenty hertz, and the upper note's second harmonic sits just below it, and those two beat. Predicted rate: one point four nine pulses a second. Measured off the render, inside a filter centred on thirteen hundred and twenty hertz: one point four nine. The chart you are about to see is that filter's output over eight seconds of the real render, with a playhead moving in real time against the sound. The first pass is the pure fifth and the line is flat, because an exact three to two ratio cannot beat. The second is the tempered one, and the dips are shaded — and those windows are not chosen by eye, they are every stretch where the measured envelope falls below half its own middle value.

The fifth got off lightly. The major third did not, and this is the part most explanations skip. A pure major third is a five to four ratio: four hundred and forty hertz against five hundred and fifty. In equal temperament a major third is four semitones, exactly four hundred cents — but a pure one is three hundred and eighty six point three, so the tempered third is about fourteen cents wide. That is seven times the error we put into each fifth. Four hundred and forty against five hundred and fifty four point three six five. The collision this time is between the lower note's fifth harmonic and the upper note's fourth, both near twenty two hundred hertz, and the prediction is seventeen point four six pulses a second. Measured: seventeen point four six. Here they are one after the other, pure first, then tempered. And I want to be careful about what to expect, because seventeen pulses a second is too fast to count. It does not sound like a wobble. It sounds like a slight, restless roughness — a texture rather than a movement.

There is a reason the comma is so obvious and the tempered third is so easy to live with, and it is measurable rather than a matter of taste. When two tones are almost the same pitch, it is the fundamentals themselves that cancel, so the whole sound goes up and down. That is the comma: measured depth of point nine four, out of a maximum of one. Nearly total. But when a third is tempered, the fundamentals are far apart and perfectly steady. The only thing beating is one harmonic, several times higher up and much quieter than the note it belongs to. Inside that harmonic the beating is just as deep — point seven — but as a share of the whole sound reaching your ear it comes to nine thousandths. That is about a hundred times shallower than the comma. Same phenomenon, same arithmetic, and completely different to listen to: one of them wobbles, and the other one just has a texture. Both numbers on this chart came off the renders you have been hearing.

Which brings us back to the piano, and to the thing that sounds like a provocation and is simply true. A piano tuner is not trying to make your intervals pure. They are deliberately making every fifth about two cents too narrow and leaving every major third about fourteen cents too wide, and they are doing it on purpose, everywhere, in every key. Not one interval on the instrument, apart from the octaves, is in pure tune. What you buy with that is enormous: every key sounds the same as every other key, a piece can change key in the middle and nothing collapses, and a keyboard instrument can play with any other instrument without being retuned. What you pay is a faint, permanent roughness in every third, which we are all so used to that a genuinely pure third can sound slightly strange the first time you hear one in isolation. If you have ever wondered why a barbershop quartet or a good string section sounds sweeter than a keyboard on a held chord — that is why. Singers and string players are not stuck with the compromise. They lean the notes into tune as they go.

So. Twelve pure fifths do not make seven octaves. They overshoot by twenty three point four six cents, which we derived from the ratio, generated as sound, and then measured back off the renders as six point zero zero three pulses a second against a prediction of six point zero zero three — with a control, two tones in tune, that correctly measured nothing at all. The circle of fifths is not a circle. It is a spiral, and it never closes, and essentially everything about how we tune instruments is an argument about what to do with that gap. The answer we settled on was to spread it evenly and accept a little roughness in every third, forever, in exchange for being able to play in any key. It is a compromise, and it is worth knowing that it is one. All of it was built, rendered and measured in DAW Pro. Thanks for watching.

description:
Twelve perfect fifths should equal seven octaves. They do not — and this lesson draws the gap, generates it as sound inside DAW Pro, and then measures it back off the renders.

THE COMMA
Derived rather than quoted: 1200*log2((3/2)^12 / 2^7) = 531441/524288 = 23.4600 cents.

HOW THE TONES WERE MADE
Two source files, both generated at exactly 440.000 Hz: a sine (the walk and the two A's) and a sawtooth (the fifths and thirds, whose beating lives between harmonics a sine does not have). Each is loaded as a sampler zone and retuned by the zone's TUNE control in cents. Every pitch in the film is one of those two files moved. Largest disagreement between the arithmetic and the render, across all twenty-one measurements: 0.0000 cents.

MEASURED BEAT RATES (predicted, then measured off the render)
440.000 + 446.003 Hz (the comma): 6.003 predicted, 6.003 measured, depth 0.9367.
440.000 + 659.255 Hz (the tempered fifth, at the 1320 Hz partial): 1.490 predicted, 1.490 measured.
440.000 + 554.365 Hz (the tempered third, at the 2200 Hz partial): 17.461 predicted, 17.461 measured.

THE CONTROLS
Three configurations that cannot beat, carried so the three numbers above mean something: two A's in tune (depth 0.0000), a pure 3:2 fifth (depth 0.0000), and a pure 5:4 third (depth 0.0069).

WHY ONE WOBBLES AND THE OTHER IS ONLY ROUGH
The comma beats between the FUNDAMENTALS, so the whole sound modulates (0.9367). The tempered third beats inside one harmonic, so the whole sound modulates by only 0.0093 — about 101x shallower. That is measurable, and it is why one reads as a wobble and the other as a texture.

THE FIX
Equal temperament narrows every fifth by 1.955 cents. The same thirteen-note walk in equal temperament ends on a measured 440.000 Hz — exactly the A it started on.

DISCLOSURE
The narration is a synthetic voice, generated locally. No music-generation model was used; every tone was generated and retuned by hand.
